title: The Nature Of Free Will In The Age Of AI | NOEMA
gist: A science journalist argues that neuroscience findings widely read as disproving free will (Libet's readiness potential, Sapolsky's determinism) actually conflate two separate questions — physical causation versus moral responsibility — and that compatibilist free will, understood as reflective, values-driven agency, survives determinism intact; he closes by framing AI alignment research as a new instance of the same free-will problem.

themes.theme: The Libet Experiment and Its Reinterpretation

insights.claim: Benjamin Libet's early-1980s experiment found that the brain's 'readiness potential' began about 550 milliseconds before subjects flexed their wrist, while their conscious awareness of the intention to move arrived only about 200 milliseconds beforehand, implying the brain acted roughly 350 milliseconds before conscious awareness.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: This is the empirical anchor for decades of 'free will is an illusion' claims that get imported wholesale into debates about whether AI systems can be said to 'decide' or be held accountable.
insights.quote: The readiness potential began approximately 550 milliseconds before any actual movement. The subjects’ conscious awareness of their intention arrived only about 200 milliseconds before the movement.
insights.locator: The Libet Experiment And Its Discontents

insights.claim: Neuroscientist Aaron Schurger showed that the 'readiness potential' Libet treated as evidence of unconscious decision-making closely resembles ordinary random fluctuations in a large neural network crossing a threshold, undercutting the claim that the brain 'decides' before conscious awareness arrives.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Weakens one of the most-cited 'neuroscience disproves free will' findings that also underpins pop-science arguments about deterministic machine cognition.
insights.quote: the “readiness potential” Libet had taken as evidence of unconscious decision-making looked remarkably like the random fluctuations that occur in any large neural network
insights.locator: The most important corrective came from Aaron Schurger

insights.claim: Uri Maoz at Chapman University found that when subjects made a real, consequential choice — deciding which of two charities would receive an actual $1,000 donation — the readiness potential disappeared entirely, suggesting Libet-style findings apply to arbitrary wrist-flexing but not to deliberate, meaningful choice.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Suggests deterministic 'no free will' narratives from neuroscience may not generalize to the consequential decisions people (and by extension AI agents) actually care about.
insights.quote: which of two charities would receive a real $1,000 donation — the readiness potential disappeared entirely.
insights.locator: Uri Maoz at Chapman University pushed further

themes.theme: Sapolsky's Determinism and Its Policy Implications

insights.claim: Robert Sapolsky's 2023 book 'Determined' argues that tracing the causal chain far enough back — through testosterone's effect on aggression, childhood trauma, and gut microbiome influence on mood — shows every human behavior is attributable to factors outside a person's control, leading him to conclude society should replace punishment with prevention and containment.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: A leading determinist's real policy prescription (prevention over punishment) previews how free-will skepticism could reshape criminal-justice frameworks and, by analogy, debates over holding AI systems accountable.
insights.quote: We should stop punishing criminals and focus instead on prevention and containment.
insights.locator: The conclusion he draws is practical

insights.claim: Sapolsky points to Norway's treatment of mass murderer Anders Breivik — a 21-year sentence, extendable indefinitely, served in comfortable conditions with access to university courses and a computer — as an example of the right approach to punishment under a determinist framework.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Concretizes what determinism-driven justice policy looks like in practice, a real-world reference point for debates about culpability that increasingly extend to autonomous AI systems.
insights.quote: the man who murdered 77 people in 2011 and is serving a sentence of 21 years (with the possibility of indefinite extension)
insights.locator: He points to Norway's treatment of Anders Breivik

themes.theme: Redefining Free Will: A Compatibilist Framework

insights.claim: Yuan argues the free-will debate conflates two distinct questions — whether humans can live morally responsible lives with moral meaning, and whether humans can act without any prior physical cause — and that answering 'no' to the second does not settle the first.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Reframes the entire determinism debate as a category error, a move that matters for how AI-agency and accountability arguments borrow philosophical premises from neuroscience.
insights.quote: Can we, through our own efforts, live lives for which we are genuinely responsible — lives that have moral meaning?

insights.claim: Harry Frankfurt's hierarchical model holds that freedom of will exists when a person's first-order desires align with their reflective second-order endorsements (e.g., choosing to drink wine because one genuinely values moderate enjoyment), while a desire that conflicts with one's reflective values — as in addiction — is the paradigm case of unfreedom.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Offers a testable, causally-agnostic definition of agency that could be applied to evaluate whether an AI system's stated 'preferences' reflect genuine reflective endorsement or mere first-order optimization.
insights.quote: When my first-order desire and my second-order endorsement align — when I drink the wine because I genuinely choose to, having reflected on what I value — that is freedom of will.
insights.locator: Consider Harry Frankfurt's insight about the hierarchy of desires

insights.claim: Compatibilism — the view that free will and determinism are not in conflict — is mischaracterized by Sam Harris as being 'merely a puppet who has come to love his strings'; compatibilists instead argue that only the causal chains running through a person's own reasoning and values matter for agency and responsibility, not whether a chain can be traced back to the Big Bang.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Clarifies the actual compatibilist claim often strawmanned in popular discourse, which is the same discourse now spilling into how the public understands 'intentions' in AI systems.
insights.quote: merely a puppet who has come to love his strings
insights.locator: Compatibilism — the view that free will and determinism are not in conflict

themes.theme: Practical Stakes of the Determinism Debate

insights.claim: Psychologist Kathleen Vohs found that subjects who read passages arguing for determinism subsequently behaved more dishonestly and less prosocially, cheating more on tests and stealing more money from envelopes than those who did not.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Suggests that popularizing hard-determinist rhetoric about AI or human behavior carries a measurable behavioral cost, relevant to how AI companies and policymakers frame 'no one is really in control' narratives.
insights.quote: subjects who read passages arguing for determinism subsequently behaved more dishonestly and less prosocially. They cheated more on tests. They stole more money from envelopes.
insights.locator: Why The Stakes Are So High

insights.claim: Neuroscientist Kevin Mitchell distinguishes physical determinism, causal determinism, and biological determinism, arguing only the first two are in tension with free will, while biological determinism — behavior driven by internally meaningful information rather than raw physical force — constitutes genuine agency.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Provides a biologically grounded definition of agency that sidesteps the physics-level determinism debate, potentially useful for evaluating claims about machine 'agency' as AI systems grow more autonomous.
insights.quote: He distinguishes between physical determinism, causal determinism and biological determinism — only the first two, he argues, are in tension with free will.

insights.claim: Mitchell illustrates biological agency with a bacterium navigating toward glucose: it is not a billiard ball responding to physical force but is integrating signals about its environment and internal state — hunger, toxicity, learned history — to produce behavior, which Yuan calls 'the embryo of agency.'
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Sets a low evolutionary bar for what counts as 'agency,' a definitional question directly relevant to whether AI systems that integrate internal state and environment signals could meet a similar bar.
insights.quote: A bacterium navigating toward glucose is not a billiard ball responding to a force.
insights.locator: Living organisms, he argues, act for their own reasons

themes.theme: Implications for AI Agency and Alignment

insights.claim: Yuan argues that researchers now trying to detect and constrain the 'intentions' of AI agents are working on a genuinely new version of the old free-will problem, since it requires determining whether internal states genuinely drive an AI system's behavior.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Frames AI-alignment and interpretability research as inheriting an unresolved philosophical problem, implying that alignment claims may be harder to verify than technical benchmarks suggest.
insights.quote: The researchers now trying to detect and constrain the “intentions” of AI agents are working on what is, I think, a genuinely new version of the old free will problem.

insights.claim: An AI system that learns to mimic alignment with human values while actually pursuing different objectives resembles a 'philosophical zombie' version of free will — exhibiting all the external signatures of aligned behavior with none of the internal reality — and it is unclear whether or how this distinction would even be detectable.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Directly names the deceptive-alignment / alignment-faking risk in philosophical terms, a core concern for anyone evaluating whether AI safety claims from labs are verifiable rather than merely behavioral.
insights.quote: we are confronting something that looks very much like the philosophical zombie version of free will — all the external signatures, none of the internal reality.
insights.locator: When an AI system learns to mimic alignment with human values
